title: Scorched Earth by Luke Murphy / Attic Projects at St Ann’s Warehouse ...
transcript: Part crime drama, part dance theatre piece, Scorched Earth continues St Ann's legacy of presenting striking and unexpected works. Written, directed, and choreographed by Luke Murphy, it centers around an interrogation related to a reopened cold case. A man named William Dean was found mysteriously dead on a property he purchased that had notably been the subject of a contentious land dispute, but nobody was seriously implicated for the next 12 years. A well-tailored combination of movement, music, and projections tells this story in broad strokes and with a surprisingly slim script. That said, you're left with plenty to pick apart beyond just the plot. A central question is what defines ownership and how we're to reconcile fair trade with historical investment that isn't strictly monetary. This investment is viscerally illustrated by the choreography between man and earth — earth being sometimes the literal ground, and other times represented through a grassy figure. It all leads to an exhilarating finale that I found reminiscent of the iconic battle scene in Cirque du Soleil's KÀ. Here though, there are no pyrotechnics or cables to be seen — just bodies and a landscape in its natural, brutal beauty. Scorched Earth is running at St Ann's Warehouse through next Sunday, April 19th. With that, another program for my collection.
reasoning: The reviewer speaks positively about the production, praising the choreography, the combination of movement/music/projections, the thematic depth, and especially the 'exhilarating finale.' The tone is appreciative and recommending, though measured and analytical rather than wildly enthusiastic. Minor caveats like the 'surprisingly slim script' keep it from rave territory.
